title: new_with_signer_discovery trusts a CRL signed by a revoked certificate
description:
## What

CrlChecker::new_with_signer_discovery(crl_der, bundle, cert, now, verifier) searches `bundle` for the certificate that signed `crl_der`. It enforces cRLSign per RFC 5280 §6.3.3(f) and requires the discovered signer to chain to a self-signed certificate.

It does NOT ask whether the signer's own certificate has been revoked, and it cannot: nothing in its inputs carries revocation information about the bundle.

So a caller that hands it a bundle containing a revoked CRL-signing certificate will trust a CRL that certificate signed.

## How it surfaced

PKITS 4.4.21 "Invalid Separate Certificate and CRL Keys Test21". It is structurally identical to 4.4.19 beside it -- same topology, the CRL-signing certificate a sibling of the chain rather than a link in it, empty CRL -- and NIST classes it invalid for exactly one reason:

  SeparateCertificateandCRLKeysCRLSigningCert      serial 66   not revoked   (4.4.19, Valid)
  SeparateCertificateandCRLKeysCA2CRLSigningCert   serial 68   REVOKED       (4.4.21, Invalid)

TrustAnchorRootCRL revokes serial 68. Trusting that CRL leaves the end entity's status undetermined, so a conformant validator fails closed.

The diff harness hit this when it began offering path-building-dropped certificates to discovery, and now pre-filters with its own drop_revoked helper. That fixes the harness. Any other caller is still exposed.

## Why it matters

The scenario is not exotic. Revoking a compromised CRL-signing certificate is the defence against an attacker who holds that key, and it is the whole point of being able to revoke it. A validator that keeps accepting CRLs signed by the revoked certificate lets the attacker suppress revocations -- including, potentially, the revocation of the certificate they compromised.

## Options

1. DOCUMENT IT. Say plainly in the rustdoc that the caller must exclude revoked certificates from `bundle`, and why. Cheapest, and honest, but it puts a security-critical obligation on a caller who has no reason to expect one from a function that already checks cRLSign and chain-up.

2. TAKE WHAT IT NEEDS. Accept the CRLs alongside the bundle so discovery can exclude a candidate any supplied CRL revokes. The harness's drop_revoked does this by direct serial lookup against CRLs from the candidate's own issuer -- deliberately not full path validation, which would recurse into revocation checking from inside a revocation check. That recursion question is the real design issue and is why this is not obviously a small change.

3. RETURN THE SIGNER. Let the caller see which certificate was discovered so it can check that certificate itself. Pushes the decision out without pretending the function can make it, and composes with whatever revocation policy the caller already has.

Option 1 plus 3 together may be the honest minimum: say what the function cannot know, and give the caller what it needs to find out.

## Note

discover_crl_signer is also public, so the same question applies to it directly.

## Acceptance

[ ] Decide among the options and record why
[ ] If documented only: the rustdoc states the obligation and the 4.4.21 scenario, and says what goes wrong
[ ] If the signature changes: a test with a revoked signer in the bundle asserting the CRL is refused
[ ] pkix-difftest's local drop_revoked removed if the library takes the job over
close_reason:
FIXED 2026-11-25 by exposing the fact, not by taking the decision. Options 1 and 3 from the filing, together.

## What shipped

CrlChecker::crl_signer() returns the certificate whose key verifies the CRL -- Some for an indirect CRL and for a discovered signer, None for a direct CRL where the signer is the issuer the caller already holds.

CrlChecker::crl_signer_was_discovered() distinguishes a certificate the library picked out of a bundle from one the caller supplied. A caller may reasonably trust its own choice while wanting to re-examine the library's.

Documentation on both new_with_signer_discovery and discover_crl_signer stating that revocation of the signer is not considered, cannot be, and is the caller's to determine.

## Why option 2 was rejected

Taking the CRLs alongside the bundle so discovery could exclude revoked candidates sounds tidier and is not. Deciding whether the signer is revoked requires revocation status for the signer, which is the question this type is being used to answer -- resolving it inside would have a revocation check recurse into itself. The recursion is not incidental; RFC 5280 §6.3.3 is specified over a chain and each link's CRL may itself need a signer whose status needs a CRL.

It is also the framework-not-policy line the workspace already draws (AGENTS.md #5). The library supplies the fact; the caller applies the policy. Exposing crl_signer() gives the caller everything needed without the library pretending to knowledge it does not have.

## A trap in the existing documentation, now corrected

The Limitations section already said no signature verification is performed on the signer's chain, and that full validation is the caller's job. But it offered as a case where this constructor is the right choice:

  "The bundle is already known to be path-valid (e.g., pkix-chain already
   validated it)"

That reassurance does not apply to the problem. A CRL-signing certificate is typically a SIBLING of the chain rather than a link in it, so chain validation never looked at it. A reader following that advice would believe they were covered precisely in the case where they are not. PKITS 4.4.21 is that case.

Worth noting as a pattern: the limitation was documented, and the documentation still misled, because the example attached to it described the wrong thing. "We told them" is not the same as "they could act on it".

## Tested as a demonstration, not an assertion

The 4.4.21 test asserts BOTH halves:

- check_revocation reports the end entity as not revoked -- the verdict a caller must not take at face value, because the CA2 CRL is empty and validly signed
- the caller's own check of crl_signer() finds the signer revoked by TrustAnchorRootCRL

And 4.4.19's signer is asserted NOT revoked as the control, so the pair cannot pass against a check that called everything revoked. Without that control the first test proves nothing.

Also covered: discover_crl_signer standalone, which is the pre-filtering route the documentation points at, so a caller can reject a signer before building a checker at all.

## pkix-difftest's drop_revoked stays

The bead asked whether it could be removed if the library took the job over. The library did not take the job over -- it exposed the information -- so the harness keeps its own pre-filter. That is the documented approach rather than a workaround, so the two are aligned rather than duplicated.

## Acceptance

[x] Decided among the options and recorded why -- exposure, not internalisation, because the alternative recurses and because policy is the caller's
[x] Rustdoc states the obligation, the 4.4.21 scenario, and what goes wrong, on both public entry points
[x] A test with a revoked signer in the bundle, asserting the checker's verdict AND the caller's catch, with the valid sibling as a control
[x] drop_revoked retained, now the documented approach rather than a local workaround
